title: SN2 substitution
subtitle: Hydroxide displaces bromide from bromomethane

reactants.caption: hydroxide + bromomethane
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw the arrows for the single, concerted step.
hintTiers: Which species is the nucleophile, and which atom is electron-poor?
The nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon while the C–Br bond breaks, at the same time. How many arrows is that?
Arrow 1: lone pair on O → carbon. Arrow 2: C–Br bond → Br.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Both HO⁻ and Br carry negative character, so they repel. A nucleophile attacks the electron-poor (δ+) atom.
Bromine is the leaving group: it leaves with the electrons rather than attacking the carbon it is leaving.
The C–Br pair goes to the more electronegative atom, which can stabilise it: bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Octet check: carbon would now have 10 electrons. What has to leave as the nucleophile arrives?
Bromide leaves with its pair. But SN2 is concerted: what pushes electrons in on the other side at the same time?

steps.explanationAfterStep: Backside attack and loss of the leaving group happen in one concerted step, so the rate depends on both species.

mechanismSummary: SN2: one concerted step. The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, so a stereocentre would be inverted (Walden inversion).
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press)
